title: An Insult That Started a War
overview: David's gesture of sympathy to a neighboring king is taken as a spying trick, the envoys are publicly shamed, and the insult grows into a war that Israel wins against Ammon and its hired allies.

parts.label: Sympathy taken as spying (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Nahash, king of Ammon (a people east of the Jordan River), had once done David some kindness, though the Bible never says what it was. When David sent men to comfort his son Hanun, Hanun's advisers claimed the visit was really a cover for scouting the city, with nothing in the story to support that.

parts.label: The envoys humiliated (vv. 4-5)
parts.note: In that culture a full beard stood for a man's dignity, so shaving half of each beard and cutting the robes to expose the body was a deliberate public disgrace, and an insult to David himself, since envoys were meant to be safe as guests. David spared his men further shame by letting them wait at Jericho, just across the Jordan on Israel's side, until their beards grew back.

parts.label: Ammon hires an army (vv. 6-8)
parts.note: Knowing they had made themselves hated by David, the Ammonites paid for soldiers from several Aramean kingdoms (Aram is roughly modern Syria). Their own troops guarded the city gate while the hired troops waited in the open field, ready to catch Israel's army from two sides.

parts.label: Joab fights on two fronts (vv. 9-14)
parts.note: Joab, David's army commander, split his forces, taking the best men against the Arameans and giving the rest to his brother Abishai, with a promise that each would rescue the other. His words before battle combine courage with leaving the outcome to the LORD, and when the hired troops ran, the Ammonites retreated behind their walls.

parts.label: The Arameans try again (vv. 15-19)
parts.note: Hadadezer, an Aramean king already beaten by David in chapter 8, gathered more troops from beyond the Euphrates River, but David himself led Israel and defeated them, killing their commander Shobak. The kings under Hadadezer then made peace with Israel and stopped helping Ammon, though the parallel account in 1 Chronicles 19 gives somewhat different casualty figures.

think: When someone's kindness gets read as a hidden trick, what makes it so hard to tell honest goodwill from a disguised motive?
